name: Nasopharyngeal Teratoma

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiologic Diagnostic Criteria for Nasopharyngeal Teratoma

criteria.description: Presence of a nasopharyngeal mass causing airway obstruction or feeding difficulties in a neonate
Radiologic evidence (CT or MRI) of a heterogeneous mass with cystic, solid, and calcified components in the nasopharyngeal region
Histological confirmation of tissues derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm)
Ultrasound or fetal MRI detection of nasopharyngeal mass during pregnancy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a nasopharyngeal mass with characteristic imaging features and histopathological confirmation of teratomatous tissue
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is often made postnatally but can be suspected prenatally with advanced imaging.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Congenital nasopharyngeal mass causing airway obstruction
Feeding difficulties due to oropharyngeal obstruction
searchTerms: difficulty swallowing due to throat blockage

pathognomonic.symptomName: Respiratory distress in the neonatal period

common.symptomName: Cyanosis episodes related to airway compromise
searchTerms: blue skin episodes from airway blockage
turning blue due to breathing issues

occasional.symptomName: Polyhydramnios detected prenatally due to fetal swallowing impairment
searchTerms: prenatal fluid buildup due to fetal swallowing problem
recurrent pneumonia due to inhaled food or liquids

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests; no specific laboratory markers
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) may be elevated in some cases
imaging: CT scan showing heterogeneous mass with cystic, solid, and calcified components in the nasopharynx
MRI demonstrating extent of lesion and possible intracranial involvement
Prenatal ultrasound or fetal MRI detecting mass and polyhydramnios
genetic: No known consistent genetic mutations associated
Sporadic occurrence with no familial inheritance pattern
other: Histopathology confirming presence of tissues from all three germ layers
Surgical biopsy or excision required for definitive diagnosis

distinguishingFeatures: Lacks cystic and calcified components typical of teratoma
Absence or blockage of posterior nasal airway
Diagnosed by nasal endoscopy and imaging
Benign mucosal lesion without germ layer derivatives
No calcifications or solid-cystic heterogeneity on imaging

redFlags: Severe neonatal respiratory distress requiring urgent airway management
Feeding intolerance with risk of aspiration
Rapid tumor growth causing intracranial extension or neurological compromise
references: Stelow EB, et al. Nasopharyngeal teratomas: a clinicopathologic study of 10 cases. Head Neck Pathol. 2010.
Kumar R, et al. Congenital nasopharyngeal teratoma: prenatal diagnosis and management. J Pediatr Surg. 2015.
